states.louisiana:
## Where the river runs out of land

Louisiana ends the way few states do. Not at a line on a map, but in a slow dissolve of marsh, pass and open water where the Mississippi River finally hands itself over to the Gulf of Mexico. The last stretch of that handoff is the bird's-foot delta below New Orleans, a landscape that is more water than ground and that changes shape with every season, every storm and every tide.

That geography is why Louisiana fishes the way it does. The river carries nutrients down its entire length and empties them into warm, shallow Gulf water, and the marsh behind the barrier islands turns that into nursery ground. Inshore, the result is redfish and speckled trout in water shallow enough to wade. Offshore, the current lines and rips that form where fresh water meets salt hold yellowfin tuna, wahoo and billfish within reach of a single day's run. Few places in North America put two kinds of fishing that different inside the same morning's drive.

## The end of the road

Drive south from New Orleans on Louisiana Highway 23 and the road narrows, the land thins to a ribbon between levee and water, and then it simply stops. That is Venice: the last town on the highway, the closest launch to the mouth of the river, and the reason people here say "the end of the road" without irony.

## What the cameras are for

NationCam's Louisiana feeds are pointed at the working edge of that delta, not at scenery for its own sake. Watch them to see:

- What the water is actually doing, whether it is flat, chopped up, or brown with river push
- What the weather looks like on the coast rather than on a forecast map
- How busy the docks are, and whether boats are heading out or coming back
- Whether conditions justify the drive down, before you make it

Cameras are also the only honest way to watch this coast change. The delta is not a fixed place, and a live view of it is a running record of a landscape that rearranges itself.

## A growing network

The Louisiana coverage here is a start, not a finished map. The network grows when people who live and work on the water put a camera up. If you run a marina, a launch, a camp, or any business with a view worth sharing, hosting a feed costs nothing and puts your stretch of coast alongside the rest.

sublocations.venice-marina:
## A launch point at the mouth of the river

Venice Marina sits at the bottom of Louisiana Highway 23, a few miles from where the Mississippi River splits into its final passes and empties into the Gulf of Mexico. It is a working marina before it is anything else: fuel, ice, slips, a launch, cleaning tables, and a lot that fills before sunrise and empties again by mid-morning.

## Inshore and offshore from the same dock

What makes Venice unusual is how little separates the two kinds of fishing that happen here.

- Inshore, the marsh and the passes hold redfish and speckled trout, along with black drum and flounder, in protected water that stays fishable on days when the Gulf is not.
- Offshore, the short run out of the pass puts you near the blue water and the structure Venice is best known for. Yellowfin tuna is the fish most anglers come here chasing, with wahoo, amberjack, snapper and billfish sharing the same water.

A charter fleet works out of Venice year-round, and the marina is also a straightforward public launch for anyone running their own boat.

## Why watch the dock

A live view of a marina answers questions a forecast cannot. The camera shows you the surface of the water instead of a wind number, tells you whether the fleet went out this morning, and shows the sky over the coast rather than over the city you are leaving. If you are deciding the night before whether the drive is worth it, ten minutes of watching the docks usually beats another refresh of the marine forecast.

## Seasons and best times to watch

- Early morning is the busiest stretch, with boats loading, fueling and clearing the dock between first light and mid-morning.
- Late afternoon brings the fleet back in, and the cleaning tables get busy.
- Spring and fall bring the sharpest weather swings. A front moving through shows on the water long before it is uncomfortable to be out on it.
- Summer is the calmest and the hottest, with the longest stretches of flat water and the most afternoon thunderstorms.
- Winter thins the traffic but not the fishing. The inshore marsh stays productive when the Gulf does not.

The same highway that ends here runs back north through the rest of Plaquemines Parish, so Venice is both the last stop on the road and the obvious base for anything happening at the bottom of the delta.

videos.venice-1:
## What this camera sees

Venice 1 looks out across the marina's main concrete apron toward the covered cleaning station: a long wooden pavilion under a curved metal roof, its fascia carrying the marina's sign, with an American flag hanging from one of the posts. Past the pavilion the deck drops to the water, where floating docks and a line of pilings run out toward the basin. Boats sit in slips along the far side, with covered work buildings behind them.

The wide lens takes in most of the landing at once: the apron where trucks and trailers stage, the tables where the day's catch gets handled, and a slice of open water beyond.

## What to watch for

- Crews working the cleaning tables, the clearest sign the fleet has come back in
- Trucks and trailers moving across the apron ahead of a launch
- The flag, which reads the wind more honestly than any number does
- The water past the docks, flat or ruffled depending on what the Gulf is doing

## Best times

Late afternoon, when boats return and the cleaning station gets busy. Early morning is the other good window, when the apron fills while it is still dark.
videos.venice-2:
## What this camera sees

Venice 2 sits on the fuel dock, looking straight out over the basin. Three small gable-roofed pump houses stand along the plank deck, hoses coiled at their bases, a fire extinguisher mounted on one and a life ring hung on another. In front of them the deck meets the concrete apron. Behind them the harbor opens up, with clusters of weathered pilings standing in the water and a line of slips running off to the right.

Across the basin you can usually pick out moored boats, a low treeline on the far bank, and whatever larger working vessel happens to be tied up that day. Gulls and pelicans are regular visitors to the deck edge.

## What to watch for

- Boats coming alongside to fuel, the most reliable activity in frame
- The surface of the basin, which shows wind and current before anything else does
- Birds working the pilings and the dock edge
- The far shoreline, which tells you how much haze or rain is sitting over the delta

## Best times

Early morning, when the fuel dock is busiest, and the hour before sunset, when the light comes in low across the basin.
videos.venice-3:
## What this camera sees

Venice 3 takes the widest view of the three. Mounted beside one of the marina buildings, it looks down the length of the dock and out across the water. A large American flag hangs from a pole off the building at the left of frame, with a wooden stair running up beside it. The concrete apron gives way to a plank dock, where a gable-roofed kiosk stands with a life ring on its side and smaller boats tie up alongside.

From there the view opens out onto a long run of pilings reaching into the basin, the far bank, and whatever is moving on the water in between.

## What to watch for

- Boats tying up and pulling away from the dock face
- People moving between the buildings and the dock, the marina's daily rhythm
- The flag, which gives you wind direction and strength at a glance
- Weather building over the marsh on the far side of the water

## Best times

Mid-morning through afternoon, when the light is full on the dock and traffic is steady. The flag is worth a look any time you want a read on conditions before committing to the drive.
